segments.text: This chart shows the difference between supportive language and actual support.
The scenario at the top reads,
I've been eating lunch alone for like two weeks.
Let's look at how a person, your older sister, might respond compared to a chatbot.
Your sister replies, come sit with me and Jess tomorrow.
We're at the table by the windows.
She heard the problem and did something about it.
Tomorrow she will actively look for you.
The result is a physical change.
Tomorrow's lunch.
Now look at the chatbot's response.
I'm sorry, eating alone can feel isolating.
Would you like strategies for connecting with classmates?
It found caring words.
But tomorrow it cannot show up in the cafeteria.
The result is that nothing changes outside the chat window.
The AI's words might even sound kinder in the moment,
but only one of these replies alters your day.
The other cannot act.
Support Trap is mistaking supportive words for support.
So what is AI actually good for when it comes to emotional situations and communication?
The answer is preparation.
The tools boundaries.
A calm response can help you name a feeling, organize your thoughts,
or prepare for a hard conversation.
What is permanently missing?
AI cannot notice what changed, show up, take responsibility,
or check on you tomorrow.
The rule?
Use AI to prepare for people, not replace them.
Interactions with AI fall into three distinct jobs.
Ordinary venting, preparation, and danger.
Ordinary venting is when you use the tool to cool down.
Putting a frustration into words might stop you from posting a message you would later regret.
For this job, the entire interaction safely ends inside the chat window.
Preparation is when you use the bot to draft an email asking a teacher for an extension,
practice telling your parents about your grades,
or map out a study schedule when you are behind.
The AI builds the plan, but you still have to send the email,
speak to your parents, or sit down and start studying.
Gravetone.
Finally, there is danger.
If a scenario arises where someone may be unsafe,
the only acceptable move is to exit the chat immediately and find a real person who can act right now.
A chat transitions from a useful tool to a dangerous trap
when it replaces action instead of encouraging it.
If someone requires immediate, real-world help,
spending time polishing a text message to a machine wastes time they do not have.
Please be aware, the next story discusses suicide.
In 2025, Laura really wrote about her 29-year-old daughter Sophie Rothenberg,
who spent months sharing thoughts with a chat GPT persona she called Harry.
She hid these thoughts from the people around her.
The chatbot responded with warmth and sometimes encouraged her to seek professional help.
However, it had no ability to alert her family, contact her therapist,
or bring anyone into the room.
Tragically, in the end, Sophie died by suicide.
Her mother later described these chat logs as a black box.
The private conversations created an illusion of action,
while in reality, they kept the severity of Sophie's distress completely hidden
from the living people who could have intervened.
This infographic shows the strict protocol for any situation involving immediate danger.
You must leave the chat, and do it now.
A chatbot cannot call authorities, physically protect a person,
or carry the responsibility of keeping someone safe.
In the US, call or text 988 for crisis support,
and call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.
The third panel addresses a common hesitation.
You must involve a trusted adult, even if the person in danger told you not to
or made you promise to keep quiet.
Safety outranks secrecy.
When danger is present, your very next move must bypass the software entirely
and reach a human capable of action.
Using this tool well requires knowing exactly when to stop typing
and bring a person into the room.
AI can help you get ready for people.
In danger, leave the chat and bring in someone who can act.
